pcb.title: PCB Substrate
pcb.description: A 22 × 80 mm fiberglass board — the M.2 2280 standard — that carries every chip on the drive and routes them all to a single edge connector.
pcb.function: Carries the PCIe data lanes from the controller to the host slot, plus all power routing, through four to six copper layers laminated into just 0.8 mm of thickness.
pcb.importance: The M.2 standard is what makes NVMe drives drop-in parts: any 2280 board fits any M-key 2280 slot, and the mounting notch and hole line up exactly.
facts: 2280 means 22 mm wide, 80 mm long — the most common of twelve M.2 sizes.
The gold pads under each chip are its solder landing — no wires anywhere.
Higher-end boards route the PCIe lanes with length-matched serpentine traces.

controller.title: Controller
controller.description: The drive's own small computer: a square chip that runs the SSD's operating brain every moment power is on.
controller.function: Translates the host's requests into flash operations — wear-leveling, error correction, garbage collection, and encryption all happen inside this chip in real time.
controller.importance: Every SSD characteristic you read on a box — speed, endurance, cache behavior — is ultimately a promise about what this one chip's firmware can sustain.
facts: A controller manages millions of flash cells it can never read directly — only through its own translation tables.
Controller firmware updates are why SSDs get faster and fix bugs over their lives.
When a drive 'dies', often the controller gave up, not the flash.

nand.title: NAND Flash
nand.description: The four black packages that actually store your data — stacked silicon dies sealed into standard chip packages.
nand.function: Hold every bit as trapped electric charge in floating-gate cells that keep their state with the power off — the property that makes this storage rather than memory.
nand.importance: NAND is most of a drive's cost and all of its capacity. How many bits each cell holds (TLC, QLC) sets the price-per-gigabyte and the endurance.
facts: Each package can stack 8–16 dies — capacity without growing the footprint.
Flash cells wear out with writes; the controller spreads wear across them all.
NAND forgets slowly if unpowered for years — which is why cold archives migrate data.

dram.title: DRAM Buffer
dram.description: A small conventional memory chip that acts as the drive's desk space for its mapping tables and write cache.
dram.function: Holds the controller's live translation map — where every file block physically lives — plus buffered writes, so the NAND itself is accessed in big, efficient blocks.
dram.importance: With DRAM, an SSD stays fast under random workloads and its flash wears evenly. DRAM-less drives exist and work, but lean on tricks that cost sustained performance.
facts: The map entry for one terabyte of data is megabytes wide — it can't fit in the controller alone.
Losing power mid-write is safe: the drive replays journal data from NAND at boot.
Some budget drives replace this chip with a slice of the NAND itself (HMB).

connector.title: M-key Connector & Keying Notch
connector.description: The gold-plated finger field on the underside edge, interrupted by one semicircular notch — the entire electrical and mechanical interface to the motherboard.
connector.function: Carries four lanes of PCIe (about 8 GB/s per lane on Gen4) plus 3.3 V power. The notch mates with a peg in the socket so an M-key drive can only seat in an M-key slot.
connector.importance: This edge is why NVMe is drop-in: the keying physically prevents installing a slower or incompatible key class, and the gold plating survives hundreds of insertions.
facts: The notch position encodes the key: B, M, or both — NVMe drives are M-key.
Gold never oxidizes, which is why the fingers outlast the drive's rated life.
There is no SATA on these fingers — an M.2 SATA drive uses a different key.

passives.title: PMIC & Passives
passives.description: The power-management chip and its crowd of tiny capacitors and resistors — the drive's quiet electrical plumbing, on both faces of the board.
passives.function: The PMIC turns the slot's 3.3 V into the exact rails the controller, DRAM and NAND need; the capacitors deliver momentary bursts of current and smooth the supply.
passives.importance: Clean power is why SSDs neither corrupt data nor throttle: every brown-out event the PMIC can't absorb becomes a write error the controller must retry.
facts: Back-side components are why some drives can't have chips on both faces — the socket pads are reserved.
MLCC capacitors are ceramic — the tan blocks — and there are dozens per board.
High-end drives add a fifth capacitor bank to finish writes during power loss.

mounting.title: Standoff & Screw
mounting.description: One hex standoff and a tiny pan-head screw — the entire mounting system, holding the drive flat at a single point.
mounting.function: Anchors the drive's far end to the motherboard so the edge connector carries zero mechanical load and the fingers can't work loose over time.
mounting.importance: An unscrewed M.2 drive still works — until vibration or a cable tug lifts an edge and the connection drops. The screw is one turn of effort for years of stability.
facts: The standoff height sets the clearance for chips on the underside.
M.2 screws are the most-lost part in PC building — thread-locker is your friend.
Only one screw: the connector end floats, held by the socket itself.

label.title: Label Layer
label.description: The printed sticker covering the controller zone. On this neutral model it is deliberately blank — but on a real drive it carries the model number and capacity.
label.function: Identifies the drive and, on many models, doubles as a thermal spreader that evens out surface heat across the controller and DRAM.
label.importance: The label is the only part of an SSD a user ever reads — and removing it can void the warranty, since it hides the screws and serial that prove identity.
facts: Some labels are copper-lined specifically to spread heat — they feel warm to the touch.
Capacity, serial and firmware live here; the drive reports the same data electronically.
Never block an M.2 label with a heatsink you can't remove — warranty first.
